title: Fulfillment at Etsy
subtitle: Crafting a Shared Vision and Guiding Principles (2022)

content.text:
A Gap Between Roadmaps and Strategy

When I joined Etsy's fulfillment team, I noticed a disconnect. Teams had near-term roadmaps and delivery targets, but they lacked a unifying vision, something that tied their work to Etsy's broader business strategy. Without that north star, it was difficult to make confident decisions or understand how each initiative contributed to the bigger picture.

Recognizing the Opportunity

I saw an opportunity to fill that gap. Not by imposing another rigid product plan, but by creating a shared vision grounded in user research, market realities, and Etsy's brand mission. This would give teams clarity on where we wanted to evolve, while still leaving room for flexibility in execution.

Goals of the Work

The purpose of this effort went beyond documentation. My goals were to:

  • Create a vision that reflected user needs while aligning with Etsy's business strategy.
  • Define guideposts that could shape yearly and quarterly planning, ensuring continuity between strategy and execution.
  • Build consensus across design, product, engineering, and business leaders that this work was both necessary and urgent.

Leading with Influence

Because this wasn't work that had been formally requested, success depended on influence and alignment. I initiated the effort, rallied cross-functional leadership, and created the conditions for the team to see the value in stepping back from delivery to define a shared direction.

content.text:
My Role

  • Championed the need for strategic alignment with my partners, using past successes to make the case for investing time in this work
  • Designed and orchestrated a three-day workshop, including defining activities and securing a neutral facilitator so I could participate fully alongside my peers
  • Synthesized the output into enduring artifacts, a vision statement, and a set of fulfillment principles that the team could carry forward into planning and execution

Partnered With

  • Research leadership
  • Staff Designer (who facilitated the sessions)

Participants

  • GM/VP of Fulfillment
  • Product, Engineering, and Research leaders
  • Product Marketing, Analytics, and Finance leads
  • Product Design Manager

Building True Alignment

To build true alignment across disciplines, I designed a three-day workshop focused on co-creation, not presentation. Rather than coming with predetermined answers, we would work together to define our shared vision and principles through structured activities and strategic thinking exercises.

Day 1: Grounding in Research

We began by grounding ourselves in what we knew about our users, the market, and Etsy's strategic priorities. This wasn't just a data dump—it was about creating shared understanding of the context we were operating in and the problems we needed to solve.

Day 2: Strategic Thinking

The second day used a "Thinking Hats" exercise to systematically explore different perspectives on fulfillment. We looked at the emotional needs of sellers, the practical constraints we faced, the creative possibilities ahead of us, and the critical risks we needed to address. This helped us think beyond our usual functional silos.

Day 3: Vision Creation

The final day focused on synthesis and creation. We used a "Cover Story" exercise to envision what success would look like in three years, then worked backward to identify the key principles that would guide us there. The goal was to create artifacts that would endure and influence decision-making long after the workshop ended.

Our North Star

Through our collaborative workshop process, we synthesized our discussions into a clear, compelling vision statement that captured both our aspirations and our commitment to Etsy's mission:

"We believe fulfillment should feel as human and creative as the items being delivered. By putting sellers at the center of everything we build, we'll create fulfillment experiences that are reliable, flexible, and distinctly Etsy—helping creative entrepreneurs focus on what they do best while we handle the rest with care and intelligence."

This vision became our organizing principle, ensuring that every initiative and product decision could be evaluated against our commitment to supporting Etsy's creative community while delivering the reliability that modern commerce demands.

Guiding Principles for Decision Making

Beyond the vision statement, we developed a set of principles that would serve as scaffolding for roadmap planning and daily decision-making. These weren't just aspirational statements—they were practical guideposts anchored in seller needs and market realities:

  • Seller-First Design: Every fulfillment solution should reduce complexity for sellers, not add to it
  • Flexible by Default: Build systems that adapt to the diversity of Etsy's creative businesses
  • Transparent Operations: Sellers should always know what's happening with their orders and why
  • Reliable Excellence: Consistency in fulfillment builds trust between sellers and buyers
  • Distinctly Etsy: Our solutions should reflect and reinforce what makes Etsy special

These principles became a leadership tool for alignment, helping teams evaluate trade-offs and maintain consistency across initiatives.

What Worked Well

  • High Ownership: Because leaders co-created the vision rather than receiving it, they felt genuine ownership of the outcomes
  • Cross-Functional Alignment: The workshop broke down silos and created shared language across departments
  • Enduring Impact: The vision and principles continued to guide decision-making months after the workshop
  • Distributed Leadership: Success came from influence and collaboration, not hierarchical mandate

Areas for Improvement

  • More Time for Big Bets: We could have dedicated more time to exploring transformational opportunities beyond incremental improvements
  • Visual Prototypes: Adding more tangible, visual representations of our ideas might have made the vision even more compelling
  • Broader Participation: Including more front-line team members could have enriched our perspective

Key Takeaway

The most powerful aspect of this work wasn't the artifacts we created—it was the process of co-creation itself. When leaders work together to define a shared future, they become invested in making it reality. This experience reinforced my belief that the best strategic work happens through collaboration, not consultation.
